title: Ancient Babylonian Clock
intro: This reconstruction counts fixed ancient Mesopotamian time units from the most recently computed sunset. It is distinct from the Renaissance European Babylonian-hours convention.
structure: A beru is two ordinary hours and contains thirty ush. One ush is four ordinary minutes. The nominal 24-hour day contains twelve beru; the provider numbers the current beru from one and the ush within it from zero.
example: At computed sunset the reading is beru 01, ush 00. One hour later it is beru 01, ush 15. After two hours it is beru 02, ush 00.
history: Beru and ush are attested Mesopotamian astronomical time/distance units. The implemented sunset-origin reconstruction is a specified modern model, not a reconstruction of every Babylonian epoch, locality or instrument.
model: The provider computes candidate sunset instants from the compact solar equation of time and declination, using a 0.833-degree standard horizon correction and the supplied latitude and longitude. It selects the latest valid sunset within its bounded search, floors elapsed ordinary seconds, then computes beru = floor(elapsed/7200)+1 and ush = floor((elapsed mod 7200)/240). The next rendered change is searched at millisecond resolution.
limits: The elapsed units are fixed; real successive sunsets are not exactly 24 hours apart, so the display is not artificially clamped to twelve beru. Invalid coordinates fail; a missing solar origin produces N/A rather than invented time. The seconds toggle does not add finer subdivisions. Solar events are approximate. The solar model assumes an idealised sea-level horizon and standard depression; local terrain and weather are not modelled.
